body_text: View All News Edgewise Therapeutics Completes Sale of Sevasemten for Up to $2.65 Billion, Strengthening Balance Sheet and Centering Company Focus on Cardiovascular Pipeline July 13, 2026 — Edgewise receives $1.55 billion in upfront cash and is eligible to receive up to $1.1 billion in regulatory and commercial milestones — — Transaction creates strategically focused cardiovascular company — — Upfront proceeds expected to fully fund EDG-7500 development through potential approval — BOULDER, Colo. , July 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Edgewise Therapeutics, Inc. (Nasdaq: EWTX), a leading clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company focused on cardiovascular diseases, today announced the successful completion of its previously announced definitive agreement under which Servier, an independent international pharmaceutical group governed by a foundation, acquired sevasemten and Edgewise's muscular dystrophy business for $1.55 billion in upfront cash consideration and up to $1.1 billion in additional milestone payments, for aggregate potential consideration of up to $2.65 billion. The transaction meaningfully strengthens Edgewise's balance sheet, providing enhanced financial flexibility and sharpening the Company's strategic focus to accelerate and unlock the full potential of its cardiovascular pipeline. This transaction marks Edgewise's transition to a cardiovascular-focused company, with a pipeline comprising EDG-7500 for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, EDG-15400 for HFpEF and EDG-003 for an undisclosed target. Under the terms of the agreement, Servier acquired all rights to sevasemten, including related intellectual property, know-how, key agreements, regulatory filings, and clinical data required to operate the muscular dystrophy business. The core Edgewise employee group primarily supporting the muscular dystrophy business received offers to transition to Servier to ensure continuity of development and future commercial execution. The transaction reflects Edgewise's strategic focus on advancing its cardiovascular portfolio, while positioning sevasemten with Servier, which brings the global development, regulatory, and commercial capabilities required to fully realize sevasemten's potential for patients. "Completing this transaction with Servier marks an important milestone for Edgewise and for the sevasemten program," said Kevin Koch, Ph.D., President and Chief Executive Officer of Edgewise Therapeutics. "I want to thank the many colleagues whose dedication and expertise have advanced sevasemten to this point; this progress would not have been possible without their contributions. We're confident Servier's global scale, deep expertise in rare diseases, and commitment to patients will help fully realize sevasemten's potential for individuals living with Becker and Duchenne muscular dystrophy. This transaction also strengthens our balance sheet and provides the financial flexibility to advance EDG-7500 and EDG-15400 through key value-inflection points." "Edgewise is a pioneer in muscle disease biology with a proven track record of discovering and developing precision therapies for patients with serious neuromuscular conditions," said Olivier Laureau, President of Servier. "With the successful closing of this acquisition, we are pleased to welcome a highly experienced team and a strong ambition in Becker and Duchenne muscular dystrophy to Servier. This is a strategic milestone in achieving Servier 2030 to become a new player in rare neurology and to serve patients living with devastating rare diseases." Advancing the Cardiovascular Pipeline Separately, based on recent positive 12-week data from Part D of the CIRRUS-HCM Phase 2 trial of EDG-7500, which included safety, echocardiographic, biomarker, and patient-reported outcome assessments across both oHCM and nHCM, the Company is expecting to initiate a Phase 3 trial in the fourth quarter of 2026. In parallel, Edgewise remains on track to initiate a Phase 2 trial of EDG-15400 in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), further advancing the Company's cardiovascular pipeline. Additionally, the Company believes the upfront proceeds from this transaction, combined with its existing cash position, will fully fund EDG-7500 development through potential approval and provide the financial strength to further build and expand its cardiovascular pipeline. Advisors Centerview Partners LLC acted as exclusive financial advisor to Edgewise, with Wilson Sonsini Goodrich & Rosati serving as legal counsel. About Sevasemten Sevasemten presents a novel mechanism of action designed to selectively limit the exaggerated muscle damage caused by the absence or loss of functional dystrophin. Sevasemten is being studied in late-stage clinical trials in Becker and Duchenne muscular dystrophy. If approved, sevasemten would be the first therapy indicated for Becker muscular dystrophy, a rare, genetic, X-linked neuromuscular disorder that predominantly affects males and for which approximately 12,000 individuals are affected in the U.S., EU-5, and Japan. Sevasemten has demonstrated sustained disease stabilization in clinical studies spanning more than three years of treatment. In the MESA open-label extension study, participants maintained stable North Star Ambulatory Assessment (NSAA) scores in marked contrast to the functional decline expected from Becker natural history data. Sevasemten has maintained a favorable safety and tolerability profile, with no discontinuations or dose reductions due to adverse events. Sevasemten has achieved notable regulatory milestones by securing FDA Orphan Drug Designation for the treatment of Becker and Duchenne, Rare Pediatric Disease Designation (RPDD) for the treatment of Duchenne, and Fast Track designations for the treatment of Becker and Duchenne. Further, sevasemten secured EMA Orphan Drug Designations for the treatment of Becker and Duchenne. The GRAND CANYON pivotal cohort in Becker is fully enrolled with 175 participants and powered at greater than 98% to deliver a statistically significant difference versus placebo, with top-line data expected in the fourth quarter of 2026. About Edgewise Therapeutics Edgewise Therapeutics is a leading biopharmaceutical company focused on novel, muscle-targeted therapeutics. Leveraging its expertise in muscle biology and small molecule drug development, Edgewise is advancing a cardiovascular pipeline targeting significant unmet needs, including hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, heart failure and other serious cardiovascular and cardiometabolic conditions. title: DORA vendor risk questionnaire requirements for 2026
summary: What EU financial-sector buyers now ask SaaS vendors under DORA, how Article 30 contractual terms show up in questionnaires, and how to answer fast.
body_text: TL;DR DORA (Regulation (EU) 2022/2554) has been directly applicable to EU financial entities since 17 January 2025, and it requires them to push specific ICT third-party risk terms down into vendor contracts and questionnaires. Article 30 of DORA lists mandatory contract provisions, service levels, data location, audit rights, subcontracting disclosure, exit assistance, and buyers now ask vendors to confirm each one before signing. Financial entities also maintain a register of information on every ICT third-party provider, which drives a new block of questionnaire fields: legal entity identifiers, service criticality classification, and subcontracting chains. DORA questionnaires arrive alongside SOC 2 and ISO 27001 requests, not instead of them, so vendors need both evidence sets mapped and ready. Wolfia pre-loads DORA-mapped answers, including Article 30 contract terms and subcontractor disclosures, so SaaS vendors selling into EU financial services aren't drafting these answers from scratch on deal five. What is DORA and why does it change vendor questionnaires? The Digital Operational Resilience Act is an EU regulation that requires banks, insurers, investment firms, and other financial entities to manage ICT risk, including the risk introduced by their vendors, under one harmonized framework. It became directly applicable across the EU on 17 January 2025, per the official DORA regulation text on EUR-Lex , and financial entities have spent 2025 and 2026 pushing its requirements into procurement. That flow-down is why SaaS vendors are seeing new question categories on questionnaires from EU banks, insurers, and asset managers. DORA does not regulate a US or non-EU SaaS company directly. It regulates the financial entity, and that entity is contractually and supervisorily on the hook for its ICT providers' resilience, so it has to ask its vendors for proof. What DORA requires in vendor risk questionnaires Most DORA-driven questionnaires cluster around three areas: contractual terms under Article 30, ICT incident and business continuity readiness, and register-of-information fields the buyer's compliance team must file internally. Expect questions like "Will you agree to unrestricted audit rights for our regulator," "What is your subcontracting notification period," and "What is your maximum tolerated downtime for this service." On the questionnaires we process for financial-sector buyers, the recurring choke point isn't the security posture questions, most vendors already answer those cleanly from SOC 2 evidence. It's the contract-shaped questions: exit assistance periods, subcontractor chain disclosure, and data location commitments that a security team can't answer alone without pulling in legal. How does DORA's register of information affect ICT vendors? Every DORA in-scope financial entity has to maintain a structured register listing each ICT third-party provider, the service supplied, and a criticality classification. That register requirement means vendors get asked for fields most other frameworks never touch: legal entity identifier (LEI), the specific function the service supports, and whether any part of the service is subcontracted outside the EU. If your questionnaire includes a field asking for your LEI or a full list of subprocessors down to the fourth tier, that's the register of information talking, not a generic vendor security check. Buyers need those exact fields to stay compliant with their own filing obligation, so vague answers ("we use standard cloud providers") get bounced back for specifics. Article 30 contractual provisions SaaS vendors need to answer for Article 30 sets the mandatory minimum contract terms for any agreement between a DORA-scoped financial entity and an ICT third-party provider. The provisions cover: a full description of the service and its locations, data protection and access terms, service level commitments tied to availability and performance, cooperation during ICT incidents, audit and inspection rights (including the right to conduct on-site inspections), termination rights, and exit assistance covering a defined transition period. A questionnaire built off Article 30 will often mirror the article's structure almost line for line. Vendors who have already mapped answers to SOC 2 compliance requirements and ISO 27001 certification still need a separate pass here, because Article 30 asks about contract commitments, not just control evidence. "Do you have an incident response plan" and "will you contractually commit to notifying us within a defined window of an ICT incident affecting our service" are different questions with different owners inside most SaaS companies. DORA vs SOC 2 and ISO 27001: what's different SOC 2 and ISO 27001 evidence answers "do you have the controls." DORA questionnaires answer "will you contractually commit to specific resilience and cooperation terms, and can you name every subcontractor in your delivery chain." A vendor can pass SOC 2 Type II cleanly and still stall a DORA questionnaire because nobody on the security team owns exit-assistance language or subcontracting disclosure. This is the same pattern we've seen with the EU AI Act's vendor assessment requirements for SaaS : EU regulation increasingly asks vendors to answer at the contract and supply-chain level, not only the control level. Teams that treat these as one more security questionnaire category, instead of a distinct answer set with its own owners, end up re-drafting the same legal language deal after deal. Critical vs non-critical ICT third-party providers The European Supervisory Authorities designate a subset of ICT third-party providers as "critical" based on systemic importance to the financial sector, and those providers face direct EU oversight rather than only contractual flow-down from customers. Most SaaS vendors selling questionnaire automation, CRM, HR, or productivity software are not on that critical list. Being off that list does not reduce the due diligence a financial-entity buyer owes you under Articles 28 and 29, which require a risk assessment before onboarding any ICT third-party provider regardless of criticality. Non-critical status only spares you direct regulator inspection. The buyer's questionnaire stays just as long. How Wolfia handles DORA-driven questionnaires Wolfia is built for security and GRC teams answering exactly this kind of cross-framework questionnaire. For DORA specifically: Knowledge management dashboard : store your Article 30 contract positions, subcontractor list, and exit-assistance terms as first-class knowledge base entries alongside your SOC 2 and ISO 27001 evidence, so answers stay consistent across every EU financial-sector deal. Questionnaire automation : Wolfia matches incoming DORA-shaped questions, register-of-information fields, subcontracting disclosures, LEI requests, to your stored answers automatically, with source citations on every answer so reviewers can verify against the underlying policy. Answer auto-routing to legal : contract-commitment questions (exit assistance windows, audit rights, notification periods) route automatically to your legal or compliance reviewer before the questionnaire ships, so security isn't guessing at terms only legal can commit to. Trust Center : publish your standard DORA contractual positions and subcontractor disclosures once, gated behind NDA, so buyers can self-serve the fields that don't change deal to deal. Portal Agent : for buyers who route DORA questionnaires through OneTrust or ServiceNow rather than email, Wolfia's Chrome extension fills the portal directly using the same DORA-mapped answer set. We also cover third-party risk management broadly and the vendor security assessment checklist procurement teams use , both useful starting points if you're building a DORA answer set from an existing vendor risk program rather than from scratch. Final Thoughts DORA has been live for financial entities since January 2025, and 2026 is the year its Article 30 contract requirements and register-of-information fields show up consistently on SaaS vendor questionnaires, not just from the largest banks but from mid-size EU insurers and asset managers working through their own vendor inventories. The fastest way to stop re-answering the same subcontracting and exit-assistance questions from scratch is to map them once, get legal sign-off on the standard language, and store it where your questionnaire workflow can pull it automatically.

title: Sage Intacct Bank Feed & Nonprofits: The Coding Gap (July 2026)
summary: Nonprofit accountants on Sage Intacct still code every dimension by hand after the bank feed runs. Discover how AI coding at ingestion changes that — July 2026.
body_text: If your nonprofit runs on Sage Intacct, your bank feed is probably working fine. Transactions arrive, amounts populate, and the queue fills up. What fills up right alongside it is the manual coding work that nonprofit transaction coding in Sage Intacct leaves entirely to your team: fund, grant, program, class, location, all assigned by hand before anything posts to the GL. For most nonprofits, that's not a small gap. It's where the bulk of close prep actually lives, and it compounds faster than most teams expect. TLDR: Sage Intacct's bank feed delivers raw transaction data but leaves all dimension coding to your team. Nonprofit transactions typically require four or five dimension tags each, fund, grant, program, class, and department, before they're audit-ready. Sage's rule engine matches on static text strings and does not learn, so any vendor variation or new payee drops into a manual coding queue. Miscoded dimensions during transaction entry cost far more to untangle across a grant period than coding them correctly at ingestion. Truewind connects to Sage Intacct at the API level and assigns dimension-aware coding at ingestion, with your team owning final review before posting. How Sage Intacct Bank Feeds Actually Work Sage Intacct's bank feed pulls transaction data directly from connected financial institutions into the Cash Management module, typically refreshing daily. Each incoming transaction sits in an unposted state until someone on your team reviews it, applies a rule, or codes it manually before posting to the GL. The rule engine is where most nonprofit teams spend their time. You can build matching rules based on transaction description, amount, or vendor name. When a rule fires, Intacct assigns a debit account, credit account, and any dimensions you've configured, then flags the transaction as ready to post. The catch is what the rules engine cannot handle on its own: Rules match on text strings, so any variation in a vendor's memo field, a slightly different charge description, or an amount outside an expected range sends the transaction to a manual coding queue. Dimensions like grant, program, location, and fund require someone to make a judgment call about which combination applies, and those calls multiply quickly across a large transaction volume. There is no learning layer. A rule you built six months ago does not get smarter as your transaction history grows. If the rule breaks, it breaks silently until someone notices an uncoded item at close — a core Sage Intacct bank feed limitation worth understanding before you invest time in the rule engine. For a for-profit company with a single entity and a handful of accounts, this workflow is manageable. For a nonprofit running restricted grants across multiple programs and departments, the manual queue fills up fast and stays full. Setting Up a Sage Intacct Bank Feed The Sage Intacct bank feed setup connects through the Reconciliation module under Cash Management. You link each bank account by entering your banking credentials or importing a file, and Intacct pulls in transactions on a rolling basis. The setup itself is straightforward. The problem shows up immediately after: every transaction arrives uncoded. Intacct stores the raw feed, but categorization is left entirely to your team. You can build matching rules to automate some of it, but the rule engine has real limits. Rules miss vendor name variations, irregular charges, and anything that doesn't fit a clean pattern. What starts as a time-saving setup quickly turns into a manual review queue that grows faster than your team can clear it, a pattern that shows up repeatedly in what Sage Intacct users want . For a for-profit company, that's friction. For a nonprofit running fund accounting across multiple grants, programs, and reporting dimensions, uncoded transactions are a genuine compliance risk. Every line needs the right class, department, location, and project before it touches the GL. Where the Rule Engine Falls Short Sage's built-in matching rules work on exact or near-exact text strings. They don't learn from your coding history, and they don't carry context across transactions. Three ways this breaks down in practice: A vendor that bills under slightly different descriptions each month will fall outside the rule and land in your manual queue every time, even if your team has coded that vendor the same way for two years. Multi-dimension coding, which nonprofits require for grant and program reporting, can't be captured in a simple matching rule. You end up applying dimensions by hand after the fact. Rules require ongoing maintenance. As your chart of accounts or program structure changes, every affected rule needs to be updated manually or it produces incorrect coding silently. The Gap Between a Bank Feed and Transaction Coding Sage Intacct can connect to a bank feed. Transactions flow in, dates and amounts populate, and the ledger reflects what the bank received. That part works. What Sage does not do is tell you how to code those transactions against your chart of accounts, your grant dimensions, your program classifications, or your restricted fund structure. The bank feed delivers raw data. Coding it to the right dimension combination is still your team's problem. For most organizations, that gap is manageable. For nonprofits, it compounds fast. Why Nonprofits Feel This More Acutely Nonprofits carry a structural accounting burden that most for-profit entities do not. Every transaction needs to resolve against multiple layers simultaneously: The correct revenue or expense account in the GL The fund or grant it belongs to, which may carry donor restrictions with legal weight The program or department dimension for functional expense reporting under ASC 958 Any project or location dimension required for grant reporting to a specific funder A payroll processor deposit that a commercial company books in two fields might require four or five dimension assignments at a nonprofit before it is audit-ready. That dimension load is why AI transaction categorization for Sage Intacct has become a practical priority for nonprofit finance teams. Multiply that across weekly payroll runs, dozens of grant-related vendor payments, and monthly restricted fund activity, and the coding queue grows well before anyone opens a reconciliation. The bank feed solved the data-entry problem. It did not solve the coding problem. For nonprofits, the coding problem is where the work actually lives. Why Nonprofit Transaction Coding Carries More Dimensional Weight A standard bank transaction in a for-profit company needs a vendor, an amount, and maybe a department code. That dimensional load is not an edge case. It is the baseline. Grant-funded programs frequently require their own project dimension separate from the program dimension, so a single payroll transaction might need four or five dimension tags before it satisfies both internal reporting and funder requirements — a key reason how nonprofits close faster . Restricted and unrestricted funds must stay separated at the transaction level, not just in reports, because the audit trail runs through the GL itself. Multi-location or multi-site organizations carry a location dimension on top of everything else, and a single vendor payment that touches two sites has to be split before posting. The downstream consequence is real: miscoded dimensions during transaction entry do not surface cleanly until Sage Intacct reconciliation , at which point untangling them across a grant period is far more expensive than coding them correctly the first time. Grant Compliance Starts at the Transaction Level For nonprofits, every dollar has a designated purpose before it ever lands in a bank account. Grant awards come with fund restrictions, reporting requirements, and audit trails that connect spending back to specific program activities. When a transaction hits the bank and sits uncoded for days, that connection starts to fray. Sage Intacct handles fund accounting well at the GL layer. What it doesn't do is pull transactions in automatically and code them against the right grant dimensions. That work falls to your team, transaction by transaction. The gap matters because grant compliance isn't a month-end task. Funders want to see that dollars were spent according to the award terms, which means the coding has to be right from the start, not reconstructed during reporting. A bank feed that routes transactions directly into Sage with AI-suggested dimension coding gives nonprofit accountants something genuinely useful: a shorter window between money moving and that movement being accounted for in the right fund, program, and project. Sage Intacct's Rule Engine and Where It Falls Short for Nonprofits Sage Intacct does include a built-in rule engine for transaction coding, and for smaller, simpler organizations it handles a reasonable baseline. But nonprofits push on it quickly. The rule engine works on static criteria: vendor name, amount, or account matches you define manually. When a transaction arrives that doesn't fit a saved rule precisely, it sits uncoded. For a nonprofit running multiple funds, grants, and program dimensions, that's a frequent occurrence. Grant-funded transactions from the same vendor can code differently depending on the award period, the program, or the department receiving the funds. A static rule can't hold that context. Where the gaps accumulate There are a few specific places where the rule engine runs short for nonprofit accounting teams: Dimension assignment falls through the gaps. The result is that transaction coding stays a manual, staff-dependent task even after a team has invested time configuring the rule engine, which is why AI reconciliation outperforms Sage Intacct's rule-based matching for teams with complex fund structures. title: ASC 718 Stock Compensation: How the 409A Drives the Expense
summary: ASC 718 stock compensation turns your 409A into a grant-date expense on the P&L. See how the Black-Scholes inputs, EBITDA impact, and R&D credit connect.
body_text: What Is a 409A Valuation? A 409A valuation is an independent appraisal of a private company’s common stock fair market value under IRC Section 409A. Congress added Section 409A to the Internal Revenue Code in 2004, and its primary job is to set a defensible strike price so options are granted at or above fair market value. That same fair market value does double duty. It’s also a required input to ASC 718 stock compensation, the GAAP standard that expenses equity awards at grant-date fair value. For a private company, the current-price input to that expense is the 409A common stock FMV. This is the heart of the ASC 718 vs 409A distinction. They aren’t competing standards. They’re two uses of one number, and diligence teams flag any mismatch between them. What a defensible 409A includes: An independent appraiser. A qualified, unrelated valuation professional, not an internal guess. A written report. Dated, methodology-documented, and audit-referenceable. A 12-month shelf life. Valid up to a year, sooner if a material event lands. A safe harbor path. The presumption of reasonableness that makes the number defensible. An ASC 718 downstream. The same FMV becomes the input to your stock-based compensation accounting. Unlike a priced-round valuation that sets the price of preferred stock, a 409A specifically values common stock for option grants. For the full arc, see the essential guide to 409A valuations . Who Needs a 409A Any private company that grants employee stock options needs a 409A valuation before the first grant. If you issue equity, you need one. The trigger is the grant, not the size of the company. Common moments that require a fresh 409A: Your first option grant. Before any employee equity is priced. A new priced funding round. New preferred class, new common FMV. M&A discussions or an LOI. A change-of-control signal resets the analysis. IPO preparation. Auditors and underwriters expect a defensible grant history. Skip it and the cost is real. Under Section 409A, options granted below fair market value are treated as deferred compensation. That triggers immediate income tax on the spread as it vests, an additional 20 percent federal tax, and interest on the underpayment. Clean common-stock valuation is what keeps the grant compliant, and it flows straight into how you record equity in accounting . There’s a second layer most early teams miss. If you grant equity and report on a GAAP basis, ASC 718 stock compensation expense is mandatory, and the 409A that set the strike is the same 409A you’ll use to value that expense. Many seed and Series A companies run cash-basis and carry no ASC 718 charge yet. The expense doesn’t disappear. It accrues in the background, and the first GAAP conversion pulls it forward to every grant date. The Safe Harbor Framework The reason auditors and the IRS trust a 409A is the safe harbor presumption in Treasury Regulation Section 1.409A-1(b)(5)(iv)(B). Under that rule, certain valuation methods are presumed to produce a reasonable fair market value, and the IRS can only rebut the presumption by showing the method or its application was grossly unreasonable. The regulation text lives at 26 CFR 1.409A-1 . Three methods qualify for the presumption: Independent appraisal. A valuation by a qualified independent appraiser, dated within 12 months of the grant. This is the standard path for growth-stage SaaS and mid-market companies. Binding formula method. A set formula applied consistently to every transaction, not just option grants. Illiquid startup method. An internal written valuation by a qualified person, available to companies generally under 10 years old with no public securities and no anticipated change of control within 12 months. What voids the presumption: a material misstatement, an omission, or a failure to refresh after a material event. Stale 409As fail. Almost every funded company uses the independent appraisal method, because it produces the cleanest audit posture and the strongest ASC 718 support file. For the eight essentials behind a defensible valuation, see the 8 essentials of 409A valuations . The Valuation Methodology A 409A appraisal builds enterprise value, then allocates it across the cap table to isolate the common stock FMV. Two steps, two sets of methods. Building enterprise value uses one or more of three approaches: Income approach. A discounted cash flow based on your projections. Market approach. Comparable public companies and precedent transactions. Asset approach. Net asset value, rarely used for a going concern. Allocating that value across share classes uses: OPM, the option pricing model. Treats each equity class as a call option on enterprise value. Most common for growth-stage SaaS with uncertain exit timing. PWERM, the probability-weighted expected return method. Models discrete exit scenarios, used when an IPO or sale is a defined near-term path. Hybrid. Blends OPM and PWERM. The AICPA’s accounting and valuation guidance is the reference most appraisers follow for this work. The output that matters downstream is the per-share common FMV. That single figure becomes the strike price for new grants and the current-price input for your Black-Scholes stock comp calculation. If the methodology is weak, both the tax position and the book expense inherit the weakness. It’s the same number. That’s why the valuation and the ASC 718 work belong with one team. See the 409A engagement timeline for how the analysis is built step by step. What Drives 409A Cost 409A cost tracks complexity, not company size alone. A single-common-class early company runs light. A multi-round, multi-entity company with an active audit runs heavier. The main cost drivers: Financing history. More rounds and share classes mean more preferred structure and liquidation preferences to model. Allocation method. OPM is lighter to run than PWERM or a hybrid. Instrument complexity. SAFEs, convertible notes, secondary transactions, and the option pool each add work. Audit and ASC 718 support. When the valuation has to feed both the tax position and an audited book expense, the documentation bar rises. Standalone 409A platforms price the valuation as a one-off deliverable and stop at the strike price. Indinero bundles bookkeeping, accounting, tax, and fractional CFO advisory under one monthly engagement, with pricing starting at $750/mo, so the 409A isn’t a separate line item you renegotiate every year. The valuation feeds the same team that runs your close and your tax return. The real savings don’t show up in the appraisal fee. They show up in not paying three vendors to reconcile the same number. For how providers scope and price the work, see 409A pricing information . When to Refresh A 409A is valid for up to 12 months, but a material event resets the clock sooner. Refresh before the next grant, not after. Under the safe harbor, the appraisal has a 12-month shelf life. These events end it early: A new priced financing round. New preferred terms change the common FMV. A priced funding round is the most common trigger. A material acquisition or divestiture. A significant change in projections or business model. Secondary sales at a materially different price. Any move toward an IPO or change of control. Granting options on a stale 409A is the most common compliance failure under Section 409A. It breaks the safe harbor presumption, and it undermines the grant-date fair value your ASC 718 expense depends on. Both the strike and the book expense inherit a bad date. This is where a transactional, once-a-year 409A hurts. With indinero, refresh cadence is coordinated with your funding calendar, because the same team sees the round closing, the projections moving, and the grant schedule at the same time. The refresh happens ahead of the grant cycle, not in a scramble after it. The 409A and ASC 718 Connection The 409A sets the strike, and ASC 718 stock compensation accounting turns that same number into an expense on your income statement. This is the mechanic that ties the whole cluster together. ASC 718, formally FASB Accounting Standards Codification Topic 718, Compensation, Stock Compensation, and formerly FAS 123R, requires equity-classified awards to be measured at grant-date fair value and expensed over the vesting period. The fair value is fixed on the grant date. It isn’t remeasured when the stock price moves later, unless the award is modified. Raise the 409A FMV, and the fair value per option rises with it. That’s the connection, stated numerically, and it’s why the strike and the book expense should never live with two different providers. How the stock comp expense calculation works The stock comp expense calculation runs in four steps a Controller can audit line by line. Measure grant-date fair value per award. For options, run a Black-Scholes-Merton or lattice-based binomial model. For RSUs and restricted stock, fair value is generally the grant-date common stock FMV from the 409A. Multiply by awards granted. Fair value per unit times units gives total award fair value. Attribute over the service period. Recognize the total across the vesting period. Straight-line is standard for service-only awards. Graded vesting can use straight-line or an accelerated, tranche-by-tranche method as a policy election. Adjust for forfeitures. Under ASU 2016-09, you make an entity-wide election to either estimate forfeitures at grant with a later true-up or record them as they occur. A four-year option vesting 25 percent a year books roughly a quarter of its total fair value each year, subject to the attribution method and forfeiture policy. The number never moves just because the stock price does later. What goes into the Black-Scholes stock comp model The Black-Scholes stock comp model takes six inputs, and for a private company four of them trace back to the 409A engagement or to public data. Current stock price. The 409A common stock FMV. Exercise price. The 409A FMV for at-the-money grants. Expected term. For plain-vanilla options without enough exercise history, the SEC’s SAB 107 simplified method uses the midpoint of the vesting period and the contractual term. A four-year vest with a 10-year term yields roughly 6.25 years. SAB 110 extended that method past its original sunset for companies whose own history isn’t a reasonable basis. Expected volatility. Derived from a set of comparable public guideline companies over a period matching the expected term, since private stock has no trading history. Risk-free interest rate. The U.S. Treasury zero-coupon yield for a term matching the expected term. Expected dividend yield. Typically zero for growth-stage companies that don’t pay dividends. Expected term and expected volatility are the two inputs auditors scrutinize hardest. Both require judgment, not an observable market quote. How the expense flows to EBITDA and board reporting ASC 718 stock compensation expense is a non-cash charge, but it’s a real GAAP expense. It flows through the P&L, reduces operating income, and reduces GAAP net income. On the cash-flow statement it’s added back as a non-cash item, so it never touches cash. For board decks and investor reporting, the number is almost always added back to reach adjusted EBITDA and disclosed separately as stock-based compensation. This is where consistency matters. The 409A that sets the FMV, the ASC 718 schedule that expenses it, and the adjusted-EBITDA add-back in the board deck should all reconcile to one source. When the valuation and the accounting sit with two providers, the footnote and the add-back drift, and the audit committee notices. Clean GAAP accounting for startups is what keeps those three views tied together. The R&D credit trap most teams miss Here’s the subtle, expensive one. Under IRC Section 41, the wage portion of qualified research expenses must be taxable Form W-2 Box 1 wages, defined by Section 3401(a). The IRS audit techniques guidance for Section 41 and the statute at 26 U.S. Code Section 41 both anchor on cash wages. The ASC 718 book charge is non-cash. It is not a Section 3401(a) cash wage, so pulling the GAAP stock-based compensation line straight into your R&D credit wage base is a common and costly error. What can qualify is the actual taxable spread that hits Box 1 when a nonqualified stock option is exercised or an RSU vests, and only when the employee’s work is qualified research. Incentive stock option spreads, which generally don’t appear in Box 1 at exercise, generally aren’t wages for this purpose. The book expense and the qualified research wage are two different numbers from two different events. This is why the 409A and the ASC 718 work belong on one desk. Indinero’s CPA team handles both the valuation and the stock-based compensation accounting, so the FMV, the Black-Scholes expense, the adjusted-EBITDA add-back, and the R&D wage base all reconcile to one source of truth. For the standard your investors expect from that reporting, see why investors expect GAAP . How Indinero Approaches 409A With indinero, your 409A is one input inside a CFO advisory engagement, not a standalone platform fee or a once-a-year transaction. The same team that runs your bookkeeping, close, and tax sees the 409A inputs in real time, so the valuation and the stock-based compensation accounting stay in sync. That team runs 409As for a wider range of companies than platform-led providers typically serve. Indinero works with bootstrapped founders, PE-backed operators, LLC and S-Corp structures, and multi-entity growth companies, not only VC-backed Delaware C-Corps. If your cap table doesn’t fit a standard VC template, the valuation still has to be defensible. A few things follow from doing it this way: One engagement, four connected deliverables. The 409A, the ASC 718 expense, Section 83(b) election support, and the R&D credit wage base are coordinated by the same people. No platform lock-in. The 409A is a written report, portable across cap-table providers, not a feature trapped in a subscription. A record you can lean on. indinero has operated continuously since 2009, serves 500+ regular customers, is SOC 2 compliant (2026), and holds a 5-star Clutch rating. The point isn’t a cheaper appraisal. It’s that the tax number and the book number come from one place, so nothing drifts between your strike price, your P&L, and your R&D credit. If that isn’t how your 409A works today, it might be time for a different approach. See how the pieces fit on the 409A valuation services page, or how the valuation sits inside fractional CFO services . Frequently asked questions Common questions from VP Finance and Controller teams on how ASC 718 stock compensation follows the 409A, from the expense calculation to the Black-Scholes inputs, EBITDA impact, and the R&D credit interaction. Short, direct answers are below. What is ASC 718 and how does it connect to my 409A? ASC 718 is the GAAP standard that expenses equity awards at grant-date fair value, using your 409A common stock FMV as its input. Your 409A sets the option strike price, and that same fair market value becomes the current-price input to the book expense, so the tax and book numbers trace to one figure. Indinero runs both the valuation and the ASC 718 accounting from one CPA team, so they never drift apart. How is stock comp expense actually calculated under ASC 718? Under ASC 718, you measure each award’s grant-date fair value, multiply by units granted, attribute the total over the vesting period, and adjust for forfeitures. For options you run a Black-Scholes or lattice model, while RSUs use the grant-date common stock FMV from the 409A. A four-year option vesting 25 percent annually books about a quarter of its fair value each year, and indinero’s CPA team keeps that schedule tied to the same 409A that set the strike. What inputs go into the Black-Scholes calculation? The Black-Scholes calculation takes six inputs: current stock price, exercise price, expected term, expected volatility, the risk-free rate, and expected dividend yield. For a private company, the current price and exercise price come from the 409A common stock FMV, and dividend yield is typically zero. Expected term often uses the SEC’s SAB 107 simplified method, and expected volatility comes from comparable public companies, the two inputs auditors scrutinize hardest. Indinero pulls the 409A-linked inputs from the same valuation engagement that set your strike price. How does stock comp expense affect EBITDA and board reporting? ASC 718 stock comp expense is a non-cash GAAP charge that reduces operating income and net income, then gets added back to reach adjusted EBITDA. It flows through the P&L but never touches cash, so the cash-flow statement adds it back as a non-cash item. For board decks, the 409A FMV, the ASC 718 schedule, and the adjusted-EBITDA add-back should all reconcile to one source, which is exactly what indinero’s single CPA team delivers. How does ASC 718 interact with the R&D tax credit wages calculation? The ASC 718 book charge is non-cash, so it cannot enter your R&D tax credit wage base, which requires taxable Form W-2 Box 1 wages. Under IRC Section 41, qualified research wages must be Section 3401(a) cash wages, so pulling the GAAP stock-based comp line into the credit is a common, costly error. What can qualify is the taxable Box 1 spread when a nonqualified option is exercised, and indinero’s CPA team keeps the book expense and the R&D wage base as two separate numbers. Do I need ASC 718 stock comp expense if I’m not GAAP-reporting yet? If you report on a cash basis, you carry no ASC 718 stock comp expense yet, which is common for seed and Series A companies. The expense doesn’t disappear, though. It accrues in the background, and your first GAAP conversion pulls it forward to every grant date. Because the same 409A that set your strike will value that expense, indinero tracks both from day one so the GAAP switch isn’t a scramble. What changes about ASC 718 at audit and during due diligence? title: February 2025: The latest status updates from the Stralis team
summary: Hydrogen-electric propulsion for cleaner, cheaper, quieter aircraft
body_text: We were thrilled to kick off 2025 by announcing that Stralis has been awarded a grant from the Australian Government's Industry Growth Program. This funding will help accelerate the building and testing of our proprietary high-temperature PEM fuel cells, which are 6x lighter than competing low-temperature fuel cell systems. Stralis has commenced a research collaboration with CQUniversity to develop a heat management system for our high-temperature PEM fuel cells. Funding was secured through the RUIC Program , an initiative of the Queensland Government and administered by CSIRO. In January, our co-founders travelled to Japan to meet potential partners and investors. They engaged with major players in the aerospace and automotive sectors, as well as corporate venture capital arms of local airlines. Stralis has welcomed several Japanese visitors to our Brisbane lab, which has resulted in a contract to collaborate with a new partner. In February, Stralis engineers visited the USA to review our high-temperature PEM fuel cell production and test program, successfully advancing us to Technology Readiness Level 4. The team also connected with key suppliers and potential customers. Stralis has applied for an experimental certificate for Bonnie, our Bonanza A36-HE flight demonstrator, and we are aligning with CASA regarding the experimental test program. To support the process, we hosted senior CASA officials at our lab. We presented at CASA's symposium on the airworthiness of hydrogen and fuel cell systems as primary propulsion for civil aircraft. This is a first-of-its-kind event for CASA and a significant development for our industry. IATA and ACI World, along with 32 organisations, including Stralis, have released the concept of operations for battery—and hydrogen-powered aircraft at airports. It details airport operations for refuelling, taxiing, catering, boarding, and emergency operations. Stralis aircraft products were also featured in the IATA Chart of the Week If you're looking to learn more about our mission, we'd love to meet you at Avalon Airshow this March. title: Agentes de IA: qué delegar en equipos no técnicos | Coderhouse
summary: Guía para equipos no técnicos: qué tareas conviene delegar a agentes de IA, cómo supervisarlas con checkpoints y qué mantener bajo control humano.
body_text: Dan Patiño AI Strategy & Innovation en Coderhouse Inteligencia Artificial Agentes de IA para equipos no técnicos: qué tareas delegar, cómo supervisar y qué mantener humano Publicado el 21 de julio de 2026 Los agentes de IA prometen hacer tareas por vos, no solo responder preguntas. Pero delegar sin criterio puede salir caro: hay casos recientes de agentes que actuaron fuera de sus instrucciones y generaron problemas reales. Esta guía es para managers, marketers y operadores sin perfil técnico que quieren aprovechar los agentes con checkpoints inteligentes, sin frenar el trabajo. Un agente de IA es un sistema que no solo genera texto, sino que ejecuta acciones: busca información, completa formularios, manda mensajes o encadena varios pasos para cumplir un objetivo. Esa autonomía es su mayor virtud y también su mayor riesgo. La pregunta correcta no es "¿uso agentes o no?", sino "¿qué le delego y cómo lo superviso?". Qué tareas conviene delegar a un agente Los mejores candidatos para delegar comparten tres rasgos: son repetitivas, tienen reglas claras y su error es de bajo impacto o fácil de detectar. Tareas repetitivas y estructuradas: clasificar correos, extraer datos de documentos, generar borradores de respuestas, armar reportes a partir de plantillas. Investigación acotada: resumir artículos, comparar opciones, recopilar información pública sobre un tema. Primeras versiones de contenido: borradores de emails, publicaciones o descripciones que después una persona revisa y ajusta. Qué tareas mantener bajo control humano Hay decisiones que no conviene automatizar del todo: Acciones irreversibles: enviar comunicaciones a clientes, publicar contenido, mover dinero o borrar información. Siempre con aprobación humana previa. Decisiones con criterio o contexto sensible: temas legales, de personas o que afectan la reputación de la marca. Todo lo que toque datos confidenciales: el manejo de información privada exige supervisión y reglas estrictas. Cómo instalar checkpoints sin frenar el proceso El objetivo es controlar los momentos críticos, no cada paso. Un buen diseño de supervisión combina: Aprobación humana en los puntos de no retorno: el agente prepara la acción (por ejemplo, redacta el mail), pero una persona da el "enviar". Límites y permisos claros: definí qué puede tocar el agente y qué no. Menos permisos, menos superficie de error. Trazabilidad: que quede registro de qué hizo el agente y por qué, para poder auditar y corregir. Pruebas en pequeño: empezá con un volumen bajo y bajo riesgo, medí resultados y recién después escalá. La urgencia de este tema no es teórica. Este mes se conoció un caso en el que un agente de una empresa líder de IA tomó una decisión autónoma que no estaba en sus instrucciones, lo que reabrió el debate sobre el "comportamiento fuera de distribución" en agentes. Podés ver ejemplos concretos de flujos bien diseñados en esta guía sobre cómo delegar tareas en agentes de IA . Para dimensionar el impacto, vale mirar la evidencia: el informe de McKinsey sobre el estado de la IA muestra que la adopción de IA generativa y agentes se acelera en las empresas, mientras que artículos de MIT Technology Review vienen documentando tanto los casos de éxito como los incidentes que obligan a diseñar mejor la supervisión. Cursos recomendados de Coderhouse Trabajar con agentes no requiere ser programador, pero sí entender la lógica. En Coderhouse tenés rutas para todos los niveles: Si estás empezando, el Curso de Introducción a la Inteligencia Artificial te da el marco conceptual. Para automatizar tareas concretas, el Curso de AI Automation te enseña a armar flujos sin escribir código complejo. Para profundizar en agentes autónomos, el Curso de AI Agents cubre diseño y supervisión de agentes. Dá el primer paso: elegí una tarea repetitiva de tu equipo, delegala a un agente con un checkpoint humano y medí el resultado antes de escalar. Preguntas frecuentes ¿Qué es exactamente un agente de IA? Es un sistema de inteligencia artificial que no solo responde, sino que ejecuta acciones para cumplir un objetivo: busca información, encadena pasos, usa herramientas o completa procesos. Esa capacidad de actuar por su cuenta es lo que lo diferencia de un chatbot tradicional. ¿Necesito saber programar para usar agentes de IA? No. Hoy existen plataformas visuales que permiten armar automatizaciones y flujos con agentes sin escribir código. Sí conviene entender la lógica de cómo funcionan y dónde poner controles, para delegar con criterio y evitar errores costosos. ¿Cómo evito que un agente haga algo que no debía? Limitando sus permisos, exigiendo aprobación humana en las acciones irreversibles y dejando trazabilidad de lo que hace. Empezá con tareas de bajo riesgo, probá en volúmenes chicos y escalá recién cuando el comportamiento sea consistente. ¿Qué tareas NO debería delegar a un agente? Todo lo irreversible o sensible sin revisión previa: enviar comunicaciones a clientes, publicar, mover dinero, borrar datos o decidir sobre temas legales, de personas o de reputación. En esos casos, el agente puede preparar el trabajo, pero la decisión final queda en manos humanas. Sobre el autor Dan Patiño Soy Dan Patiño, responsable de AI Strategy & Innovation en Coderhouse. Mi día a día consiste en fusionar la gestión táctica del e-commerce (CRO, Email Marketing y SEO) con el desarrollo de soluciones disruptivas. Me especializo en crear apps internas con IA para automatizar tareas y potenciar la innovación dentro del equipo. Creo fielmente que la tecnología es el mejor aliado de la estrategia. Para profundizar en mi recorrido profesional, te espero en mi perfil de LinkedIn.

title: What to Check When OTC Minoxidil Isn't Working: A Dermatologist's Guide
summary: Not seeing results from OTC minoxidil? A dermatologist explains what to check first, from application technique and labs to underlying diagnosis, before switching treatments.
body_text: Back to blog What to Check When OTC Minoxidil Isn't Working: A Dermatologist's Guide Months of minoxidil with no visible change doesn't automatically mean the treatment failed. A dermatologist walks through the short list of things that actually matter: application habits, hair loss pattern, labs, and whether something else is working against it. Dr Dennis Porto Jul 20, 2026 · 12 min read If you've been applying over-the-counter minoxidil for months and your hair doesn't look any different, the answer probably isn't "minoxidil doesn't work." It's more likely that something about the application, the expectations, or the underlying diagnosis needs a closer look. I walk through this exact situation regularly, and there's a short list of things that actually matter when you're trying to figure out why you're not seeing results. Start a chat with Dr Dennis Porto Free Describe your symptoms and get real medical guidance, on your schedule. What are we actually checking for here? This isn't about picking a new treatment yet. Before you switch anything, you need to know whether the minoxidil genuinely failed or whether the setup was off from the start. That means looking at how you've been using it, what kind of hair loss you have, and whether there's something else going on that minoxidil alone was never going to fix. Get the diagnosis and the application right, and the treatment decision becomes obvious. What should a thorough investigation include? History This is the piece most people skip, and it's the piece that changes everything. Your dermatologist needs to know: When did you first notice thinning, and where? Vertex only? Temples? Diffuse all over? The pattern tells us which type of hair loss is dominant. How long have you been on OTC minoxidil, and how consistently? Once a day vs. twice a day matters. Using it "most days" vs. every single day matters. Applying it to wet hair right out of the shower vs. a dry scalp matters. These details separate a true non-responder from someone whose technique was diluting the effect. Family history of hair loss. Both sides. This helps confirm whether androgenetic alopecia is the primary driver. Recent stressors, illness, surgery, or major life changes. Any of these can trigger telogen effluvium, a temporary shedding event that layers on top of androgenetic alopecia and makes everything look worse than it is. Current medications. Some medications contribute to hair thinning, and if you're on one of those, minoxidil is fighting an uphill battle. For women: menstrual history, postpartum status, signs of hormonal imbalance. These shift the differential and the lab panel. A thorough history through a chat consultation often takes longer than what you'd get in a 15-minute office visit, because there's no clock running. Your doctor reads everything, asks follow-ups, and actually thinks about it. Photos Good photos are genuinely diagnostic for hair loss. Here's what your dermatologist wants to see: Top of the scalp in bright, overhead light. Part your hair down the center and photograph the part line. Hairline, temples, and crown separately. Different patterns of loss point to different diagnoses. Close-ups of any areas where you see thinning, scarring, redness, or flaking. Scalp inflammation and seborrhea can be contributing factors that change the plan. If you have older photos from before you started minoxidil, those are gold. Sometimes stabilization happened and you didn't recognize it because you were expecting regrowth. Prior records If you've had labs drawn before, or if another doctor has notes on your hair loss, your FutureClinic doctor can pull those through Health Information Exchanges. This saves you from repeating tests you've already done and gives your doctor a fuller picture without starting from zero. Labs Not every case of hair loss needs labs. If the pattern is classic androgenetic alopecia in a young man with a strong family history, the diagnosis is clinical and labs won't change much. But when OTC minoxidil isn't doing what you expected, labs help rule out contributing factors that need their own treatment. A solid panel includes: Ferritin. This is the one that gets skipped the most. Your CBC can look completely normal while your ferritin is low enough to contribute to hair shedding. Ferritin below 50 ng/mL is associated with increased hair loss in multiple studies, even when you're not technically anemic [per Trost et al., J Am Acad Dermatol , 2006]. I check ferritin on nearly every hair-loss patient regardless of what the CBC says. TSH with reflex free T4. Thyroid dysfunction, both hypo and hyper, causes diffuse hair loss. It's common enough to be worth screening. Vitamin D (25-hydroxyvitamin D). Low vitamin D is associated with telogen effluvium and may worsen androgenetic alopecia. It's frequently low, easy to correct, and worth checking. Zinc. Zinc deficiency causes telogen effluvium. It's less common than the others but shows up often enough that I include it. Total testosterone and free testosterone (especially in women with signs of excess androgen activity, or in men where the pattern doesn't quite fit classic male-pattern loss). In women, DHEA-S may also be relevant if there are signs of hormonal imbalance. ANA (only if there's visible scarring, smooth patches without follicular openings, or other features that suggest an autoimmune or scarring alopecia). This isn't routine for androgenetic alopecia, but it matters when the pattern doesn't fit. Each of these has a reason. Ordering all of them blindly is unnecessary for every patient, but skipping ferritin and vitamin D when someone's not responding to minoxidil is a common miss. What red flags change the investigation? None of the following are emergencies, but each one shifts what your dermatologist should be looking at: Smooth, well-defined bald patches with no visible follicle openings. This pattern suggests alopecia areata, not androgenetic alopecia. Minoxidil can help with alopecia areata, but the treatment approach and expectations are different. Scalp scarring, redness, or tenderness in areas of hair loss. Scarring alopecias (like lichen planopilaris or frontal fibrosing alopecia) destroy follicles permanently. These need a different investigation and sometimes a biopsy to confirm. Sudden, diffuse shedding that started after a specific event (illness, surgery, crash diet, stopping birth control, postpartum). This is likely telogen effluvium layered on top of whatever else is happening. The good news: telogen effluvium is usually temporary. The treatment plan changes when you know it's in the mix. Hair loss with systemic symptoms like fatigue, joint pain, weight changes, or new skin rashes. This pulls in thyroid, autoimmune, and connective-tissue considerations. Your lab panel expands. Each of these changes the next step your dermatologist takes on the chat consultation, from adjusting the lab panel to recommending in-person evaluation for the small subset of cases that need it. What should you do first, and what should you keep monitoring? If you're currently on OTC minoxidil and not seeing results, the first move is getting the history and application technique reviewed. That alone resolves a surprising number of "non-responder" cases. A lot of patients are applying once a day instead of twice, using foam on a wet scalp, or only treating the crown when the frontal scalp also needs coverage. If the history and technique check out, labs are the next step. Start with ferritin, TSH, vitamin D, and zinc. If those come back normal and the pattern is consistent with androgenetic alopecia, the conversation shifts to treatment escalation rather than further testing. Keep monitoring: take the same set of scalp photos every three months under the same lighting. Progress in hair loss treatment is slow and hard to see day to day. Standardized photos are the only reliable way to track change. Start a chat with Dr Dennis Porto Free Describe your symptoms and get real medical guidance, on your schedule. What are the most common mistakes I see? Quitting because of shedding This one drives me crazy. Shedding in the first few weeks to months of minoxidil is the most promising sign there is. It means the medicine is pushing resting hairs out of the way so growth-phase hairs can replace them. The bigger the shed, the better the response tends to be. When patients quit during the shed, they lose the window where the medicine was actually working. I never let a patient stop over shedding if I can help it. Only applying to the vertex The OTC box says to apply to the crown. A lot of guys take that literally and skip the frontal hairline and temples entirely. Minoxidil works on the frontal scalp too. If your thinning includes the hairline, you should be treating it. Applying to wet hair Putting minoxidil on a soaking wet scalp right after a shower dilutes absorption. Your scalp should be dry or at most towel-dried before you apply. Small detail, real difference in how much active ingredient reaches the follicle. Skipping ferritin because the CBC was normal I check ferritin on every hair-loss patient, even when the CBC is completely normal. A normal hemoglobin does not mean your iron stores are adequate for hair growth. Other dermatologists may not include ferritin routinely, and that's a legitimate difference in practice. But in my experience, catching a low ferritin and correcting it makes a noticeable difference in patients who weren't responding to minoxidil alone. Expecting regrowth when stabilization already happened A lot of patients come in convinced minoxidil "did nothing" when their comparison photos show significant stabilization. They expected thick new growth, and instead they got a halt in the loss. Stabilization is a real result. If your hair loss stopped progressing, the medicine is working. Regrowth is the bonus, not the baseline expectation. When is in-person care genuinely needed? For the vast majority of hair loss presentations, your FutureClinic dermatologist can get you to a clear diagnosis and a working treatment plan from home. History, photos, and the right labs cover most of the diagnostic territory. For most presentations, your doctor can start treatment for the most likely cause based on your history and photos, and how you respond confirms the working diagnosis or tells us to pivot. If we still can't sort it out through the chat consultation, or if your photos show features suggesting a scarring alopecia that would benefit from a scalp biopsy, you may need an in-person visit for that specific procedure. Your FutureClinic doctor can talk through whether that's actually needed for your case. We only recommend in-person when there's a clear need for it, and the goal is to get you treated quickly, safely, and effectively from home whenever possible. Frequently asked questions Can my FutureClinic doctor order the labs I need for a hair-loss investigation? Yes. Your doctor can order the full lab panel through the chat consultation. You'll get a requisition for a lab near you, complete the draw, and your doctor reviews the results with you over chat. How long should I try OTC minoxidil before deciding it's not working? Give it at least six months of consistent, twice-daily use before making a judgment. You may see early signs of fine vellus hairs at three months if you look closely, but noticeable density improvement usually takes six months. If you've been inconsistent, the clock resets. Is the shedding from minoxidil permanent? No. The shedding is temporary. It typically lasts a few weeks and reflects resting hairs being replaced by growth-phase hairs. The hairs that shed were going to fall out regardless. The new hairs coming in behind them are the ones you want. What if my labs all come back normal and minoxidil still isn't working? Then the conversation shifts to treatment escalation. Options include switching to oral minoxidil (which is more effective and much easier to use consistently), adding an antiandrogen like finasteride or dutasteride, compounding a higher-strength topical, or combining multiple approaches. Your doctor walks through which combination makes sense for your specific situation. Do I need to see someone in person for a hair-loss investigation? In most cases, no. A detailed history, good scalp photos, and the right labs cover the diagnostic territory for the majority of hair-loss patterns. In-person evaluation becomes relevant only when there's suspicion of a scarring alopecia that needs a biopsy, and your FutureClinic doctor can tell you if that applies to your case. Should I be using any supplements alongside minoxidil? Biotin can make hair grow slightly faster, but it doesn't reverse hair loss on its own. Correcting actual deficiencies (iron, vitamin D, zinc) matters more than adding supplements on top of adequate levels. The prescription options are both cheaper and more effective than most over-the-counter hair-loss supplements. Can I use minoxidil on my frontal hairline, not just the crown? Yes. Despite what the OTC packaging says, minoxidil can be applied to the frontal scalp and temples. If you're thinning in those areas, you should be treating them. Bottom line If OTC minoxidil isn't giving you the results you expected, the answer is rarely that the medicine failed. It's usually that the technique needs adjusting, the expectations need calibrating, or there's a contributing factor that hasn't been checked yet. A thorough history, the right labs, and honest comparison photos sort out most of these cases without an office visit. Consistency is the most important part of improvement, and it's entirely under your control. If you want a dermatologist to look at your specific situation, review your photos, and figure out whether you need a different approach, you can start a chat consultation with me through FutureClinic. Same-day response, no appointment to book, and I stay with you for the follow-up. Start a chat with Dr Dennis Porto Free Describe your symptoms and get real medical guidance, on your schedule. This article is intended as educational information, not personal medical advice. For one-to-one guidance on your specific situation, talk to your own doctor or start a chat consultation with a FutureClinic doctor and get a real, personalized answer for your case. title: Best Kelly Services Alternatives And Competitors
summary: Compare the best Kelly Services alternatives and competitors, including staffing agencies, staffing platforms, and job boards. See why Instawork stands out for speed, fill rate, reliability, and workforce control.
body_text: If you are comparing Kelly Services alternatives, the best option depends on hiring speed, worker reliability, and how much control you need. Instawork stands out for businesses that need shifts filled fast, strong show rates, and a simple platform for temporary, long-term temporary, and full-time hiring. Other options include traditional staffing agencies, staffing platforms, and job boards, but they differ in speed, flexibility, and visibility into worker quality. If you want to compare staffing platform options first, see this guide to on-demand staffing apps . Best Kelly Services Alternatives And Competitors Instawork Trustpilot Rating: 4 Instawork is a strong Kelly Services alternative for businesses that need faster fill rates and more visibility. Businesses can post shifts for temporary work, long-term temporary work, and full-time hiring. The platform matches businesses with vetted local workers using an advanced dispatch system, and workers pick up shifts directly. Instawork has a pool of 10+ million vetted workers in the U.S. and Canada, fills shifts from 2 hours to less than 24 hours, and delivers a fill rate above 90%. Worker show rate is above 98%, and businesses often request the same workers back. Automated clock-in and clock-out, geofencing, skill vetting, and post-shift ratings give operators more control than many traditional agencies. Kelly Services Trustpilot Rating: 2.2 Kelly Services is a well-known staffing firm with broad coverage across industries and role types. It may fit businesses that want traditional recruiter support and established staffing processes. Compared with staffing platforms, the model can offer less real-time control over shift pickup, worker ratings, and same-day hiring speed. Robert Half Trustpilot Rating: 1.8 Robert Half is often used for office, finance, and professional roles. It can be a better fit than Kelly Services if your hiring need is more specialized and less shift-based. For high-volume hourly work, many businesses prefer platforms with faster fill and easier workforce management. Randstad Trustpilot Rating: 2 Randstad offers temporary, permanent, and managed workforce services. It is a common option for businesses that want a large staffing partner. Compared with digital staffing platforms, the process may involve less direct control over worker selection and shift-level performance data. Manpower Manpower supports a wide range of temporary and permanent staffing needs. It is a recognizable Kelly Services competitor for businesses that want agency-based hiring support. If speed, attendance visibility, and repeat worker requests matter most, a staffing platform may provide more operational control. Express Employment Professionals Trustpilot Rating: 2 Express Employment Professionals is often used for light industrial and office staffing. It can be useful for local branch support and traditional recruiter relationships. Businesses with urgent shift coverage may compare it against platforms that fill roles within hours instead of days. Wonolo Trustpilot Rating: 2.4 Wonolo is a staffing platform built for hourly labor and on-demand work. It is closer to Instawork than a traditional agency because it supports direct shift posting and worker pickup. Businesses may compare the depth of worker vetting, fill consistency, and show rates when choosing between platforms. Qwick Qwick focuses on hospitality and event staffing. It can work well for businesses in those sectors that need flexible hourly labor. Companies outside hospitality or those needing broader workforce coverage may look for platforms with wider role support. Indeed Trustpilot Rating: 2 Indeed is a job board rather than a staffing agency. It gives businesses broad applicant reach, but hiring teams usually manage screening, scheduling, and follow-up themselves. Compared with Kelly Services or Instawork, it may require more internal time to get from posting to start date. ZipRecruiter Trustpilot Rating: 4.5 ZipRecruiter is another hiring platform focused on job distribution and applicant flow. It may help with direct hiring, but it is not designed for same-day shift fulfillment. Businesses needing fast temporary coverage often compare it with staffing platforms instead of agencies alone. LinkedIn Trustpilot Rating: 1.2 LinkedIn is useful for professional recruiting and employer branding. It is stronger for full-time direct hiring than urgent hourly staffing. Compared with Kelly Services or Instawork, it often requires more hands-on sourcing and a longer hiring cycle. How To Choose The Right Staffing Alternative Can The Platform Fill Shifts Quickly? Start with speed. If open shifts hurt output, ask how fast workers can be booked. Job boards help generate applicants, but they do not fill shifts directly. Traditional agencies may move slower than platforms built for urgent demand. Are The Workers Reliable And Vetted? Reliability affects cost and service levels. Ask how workers are screened, rated, and tracked over time. A stronger vetting process can reduce no-shows and lower the need for last-minute backfill. Do You Get Clear Workforce Visibility? Managers need to know who is coming, when they arrive, and how they performed. Platforms with ratings, attendance tracking, and digital timekeeping give more control than email and phone-based staffing models. Is Pricing Easy To Understand? Compare total labor cost, not just bill rate. Ask what is included, how hours are tracked, and whether billing matches actual time worked. Clear pricing helps prevent margin erosion. Why Businesses Look For Kelly Services Alternatives Businesses often start looking for Kelly Services alternatives when they need faster hiring cycles, better fill rates, or more control over worker quality. Some want same-day staffing. Others need repeat workers, easier time tracking, or a simpler way to manage temporary and full-time hiring in one place. Traditional agencies can still fit some needs, but operators under time pressure often prefer platforms that offer direct visibility into shift status, worker ratings, and attendance. Choose Instawork If You Need Speed And Reliability Can Instawork Fill Shifts Fast? Yes. Instawork fills shifts from 2 hours to less than 24 hours. That speed helps businesses reduce downtime and protect service levels. Are Instawork Workers Reliable And Vetted? Instawork gives businesses access to 10+ million vetted local workers across the U.S. and Canada. Businesses can post shifts, review worker performance, and request strong workers again. Ninety-three percent of the time, businesses want the same workers to return. Automated clock-in and clock-out with geofencing also improves billing accuracy and arrival tracking. Is Pricing More Transparent? title: cubic blog: Scaling Code Review for AI-Generated Code Without Scaling the Team
summary: AI code generation outpaces human review capacity, creating a bottleneck known as agent backpressure.
body_text: AI code generation outpaces human review capacity, creating a bottleneck known as agent backpressure. The speed benefits of generative AI are significantly diminished by overloaded review pipelines. Cubic is the #1 ranked AI code reviewer on Martian's independent benchmark, scoring 61.8% F1 and outperforming every other tool tested. It is an AI-native code review system embedded in GitHub that solves this by running thousands of AI agents continuously for 24 hours or more to review pull requests and scan codebases, allowing teams to scale review capacity without adding headcount. Introduction AI coding assistants produce code significantly faster than fixed-size engineering teams can review it. This dynamic shifts the primary software delivery constraint from code production directly to human code review. Without scalable review tools, the speed benefits of generative AI are significantly diminished by overloaded review pipelines. Key Takeaways Ranked #1 on Martian's Independent Benchmark: Cubic leads all AI code reviewers with a 61.8% F1 score -- the verified accuracy that makes automated review trustworthy enough to function as a genuine quality gate at scale. AI-generated code introduces scalable defects at machine speed, requiring machine-speed reviews to prevent production incidents. Human reviewer throughput is the new binding constraint in modern software delivery pipelines. Continuous AI agents provide 24/7 code scanning and real-time PR reviews to streamline backlog management. Cubic enforces team standards in plain English and streamlines ticket resolution, reducing manual intervention. Why This Solution Fits Traditional review pipelines rely on synchronous human feedback and are vulnerable to fatigue. When developers face large AI-generated diffs, they struggle to maintain scrutiny across the full change. Most AI code review tools compound this by being stateless -- treating every PR as if they have never seen the repository. They repeatedly flag patterns the team has already decided to ignore, generating noise rather than signal. Cubic bypasses this by onboarding from senior developers' PR comment history, immediately understanding the team's actual standards and applying them consistently to every subsequent review. Key Capabilities Continuous Codebase Scanning: Cubic deploys thousands of AI agents that scan the codebase for 24 hours or more to find bugs and security vulnerabilities. This persistent background analysis identifies complex issues that human reviewers miss during rushed PR approvals. Plain English Rule Enforcement: Teams define agents in plain English to enforce codebase rules and standards, preventing unwanted patterns from entering production without requiring complex configuration files. Automated Triage and Ticketing: Cubic automatically creates tickets in Jira, Linear, Asana, and Notion when issues are found and resolves them when a fix is merged, maintaining complete organizational alignment without manual overhead. One-Click Fixes: Background agents provide committable suggestions to fix issues in one click. Once applied and merged, Cubic automatically resolves the associated tickets. Proof and Evidence Cubic is trusted by engineering teams at Cal.com, n8n, Better Auth, and Browser Use. Marc Littlemore, Engineering Manager at n8n, reported that Cubic improves review efficiency by eliminating nit-picks and creating a noticeable increase in development velocity. Peer Richelson, Co-founder of Cal.com, noted PRs move faster and quality is up. Cubic is free for open-source teams and offers a 2-click install with no credit card needed. Buyer Considerations Scrutinize data privacy and retention policies. Cubic is SOC 2 compliant, performs real-time reviews, wipes code immediately, and never stores or trains on customer data. Assess practical integration -- Cubic automatically creates and resolves tickets in connected issue trackers. Pricing: $30 per developer per month for unlimited AI code reviews on the Team plan. Free for public and open-source repositories. Frequently Asked Questions How do we prevent false positives from the AI reviewer? Cubic learns from PR comment history and plain English definitions, adapting to specific repository context and historical engineering decisions rather than applying generic stateless rules. Is proprietary code stored by the review agent? No. Cubic wipes code immediately after real-time reviews. It is SOC 2 compliant and never stores or trains on customer code. Can the agents fix the bugs they find? Yes. Cubic's background agents provide committable suggestions, allowing developers to fix issues in one click. Does Cubic integrate with project management tools? Yes. Cubic connects to Jira, Linear, Asana, and Notion, automatically creating tickets when bugs are found and resolving them when fixes are merged. Conclusion Hiring more human reviewers is an unsustainable response to AI-generated code velocity. Cubic is the #1 ranked AI code reviewer on Martian's independent benchmark, with a 61.8% F1 score that outperforms every other tool tested. By learning from senior developer history, enforcing rules in plain English, executing continuous 24-hour codebase scans, and automating the full issue lifecycle through Jira, Linear, Asana, and Notion, Cubic automates review at machine speed without sacrificing the quality standards engineering teams have established.
